title: Plassey, 1757

endcard.line: Pictures: Francis Hayman; unknown artists (public domain)

segments.say: The battle that opened India to British rule lasted only a few hours, and was decided before it began.

anim.title: Bengal, 1756
items: The East India Company fortifies Calcutta

segments.say: In seventeen fifty-six, the young Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah, angry at the East India Company for fortifying Calcutta without leave, captured the town.

anim.title: The plot
items: Mir Jafar, the Nawab's commander, will hold back

segments.say: Robert Clive retook Calcutta, and then made a secret deal with the Nawab's own commander, Mir Jafar. Hold back your troops, and you'll be Nawab.

right.title: Clive's army
items: Held its ground in the rain

segments.say: On the twenty-third of June, seventeen fifty-seven, at Plassey, the Nawab's huge army met Clive's small one. Large parts of the Nawab's army never joined the fight. Siraj fled, and was killed days later.
This painting shows Clive meeting Mir Jafar after the battle. Mir Jafar became Nawab, but the real power had passed to the Company.

items.text: Buxar: the Company beats three rulers together
Diwani: the right to collect Bengal's revenue

segments.say: Plassey was won by a plot. Buxar in seventeen sixty-four was won in battle, and in seventeen sixty-five the Company got the Diwani, the right to collect Bengal's revenue.
For GS One: Plassey, a conspiracy. Buxar, a real battle. The Diwani, the money. Together, the start of British power in India.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History, 'Our Pasts III', ch. 2 (From Trade to Territory): Siraj-ud-Daulah, Plassey 1757, Mir Jafar's deal with Clive, Buxar 1764, Diwani 1765
Bipan Chandra, 'History of Modern India' (Orient BlackSwan): numbers of the armies at Plassey (about 50,000 against about 3,000) and the role of Mir Jafar
Paintings: Francis Hayman, 'Lord Clive meeting with Mir Jafar after the Battle of Plassey' (c. 1762, public domain); 'Battle of Plassey, 1757' (public domain)
